text: The Copy activity copies data from a source data store to a sink data store, among data stores located on-premises and in the cloud alike. It's genuinely the activity you'll reach for the most in this entire course — every linked service you've built so far exists mainly to feed a Copy activity moving real data between two real places.

Regardless of the actual source or sink, the Copy activity performs the exact same three-step process underneath, every single time. It reads data from the source data store. It performs serialization, compression, and column mapping, based on the input and output datasets and its own configuration. And then it writes the result to the sink data store.

The Copy activity runs on an integration runtime — the Azure Integration Runtime for two publicly accessible cloud stores, or a self-hosted integration runtime for anything on-premises or behind access control, exactly like Lesson 8 already covered. One real limit worth remembering: you can't mix two different self-hosted runtimes within the same Copy activity.

Copying into a SQL destination and the table doesn't exist yet? The Copy activity can genuinely create it automatically, based on the shape of the source data itself — a fast way to start loading and evaluating, though it's worth reviewing that generated schema before trusting it in anything you'd actually call production.

The Copy activity moves data well, but it's deliberately limited on real transformation — that's mapping data flows' job, in Chapter 5, or an external compute engine entirely. Next: exactly how far that Copy activity mapping tab actually goes, and where it genuinely stops.
